title: Dynamic arrays, structures and nested allocations
learningObjectives: Allocate an array of structures at runtime and access its members using valid array indices and structure-member operators.
Explain the difference between allocating a structure and allocating separate objects referenced by pointer members inside that structure.
Design an ownership and cleanup plan for a structure that contains one or more dynamically allocated members.
Initialize pointer members and element counts before performing nested allocations so partial-failure cleanup is safe.
Release nested allocations before releasing the outer structure, and handle partially constructed objects without leaks or invalid frees.
Choose between a single contiguous allocation and multiple nested allocations based on lifetime, ownership, resizing and data-layout requirements.
prerequisites: CL8.1 — Memory regions, allocation concepts and object lifetime

understand.concept: A program can allocate an array of structures or allocate a structure whose pointer members refer to separate allocations. These designs have different memory and ownership requirements. Allocating the outer structure does not automatically allocate the objects referenced by its pointer members. Each successful nested allocation needs initialization, a clear owner and a matching release.
understand.whyItMatters: Real programs often represent records, users, inventory items or other objects whose number of elements and text/data sizes are known only at runtime. Correct nested allocation makes these structures flexible while preventing leaks when only part of an object can be created.
understand.analogy: Imagine a folder that contains references to separate documents. Buying the folder does not create the documents inside it. Each document must be obtained separately, tracked and returned by whoever owns the folder's contents.
understand.analogyLimit: A C structure stores pointer values, not automatic ownership relationships. The language does not recursively allocate or free pointer members when a structure is allocated or released.

examples.title: Create and destroy a structure with nested allocations
examples.explanation: Expected output: `Mina: 78 84 91`. The outer structure, the name string and the scores array are three separate allocations. Pointer members are initialized to `NULL` before nested allocations. If either nested request fails, `destroy_student` can safely release whichever resources were acquired because `free(NULL)` is permitted. The helper releases nested members before the outer structure.

examples.title: Allocate and traverse a runtime-sized array of structures
examples.explanation:
Expected output:
`101: 19.50`
`102: 25.00`
`103: 12.75`
The allocation contains three complete `struct Product` objects in one contiguous array. Compound literals assign each structure value, and the loop accesses only valid indices. There are no nested pointer members in this example, so one `free` releases the entire array.

commonMistakes: Assuming that `malloc(sizeof *student)` also allocates storage for pointer members such as `name` and `scores`.
Reading a pointer member before assigning it a valid pointer or initializing it to `NULL`.
Failing to release an earlier nested allocation when a later allocation fails.
Freeing the outer structure before releasing nested resources that the cleanup code still needs to reach.
Freeing borrowed memory that the structure does not own.
Using the wrong element size when allocating an array of structures.
Assuming that freeing an array of structures automatically frees allocations referenced by pointer members.

practise.guidedTask: Define a structure containing a pointer to a character array and a pointer to an integer array. Allocate the outer structure, initialize both members to `NULL`, allocate each nested array, check each result, and write one cleanup function that safely handles partial construction.
practise.independentTask: Build a small dynamic contact list using an array of structures. Each structure should own a separately allocated name string. Support adding records, printing them and destroying the entire list. Test failure during a later name allocation and ensure every earlier allocation is released exactly once.
hints: Allocate the outer structure and each pointer member separately unless you deliberately design one combined allocation.
Initialize all owned pointer members to `NULL` before any operation that can fail.
Keep an explicit count for each dynamically allocated array.
Release nested resources before releasing the outer structure.
A cleanup helper should safely accept partially initialized objects.
Free only allocations the current structure or function actually owns.

questions.prompt: After `malloc(sizeof *student)` succeeds, what is true of `student->name` if it is a pointer member?
options: The pointer member exists, but it does not automatically point to a separately allocated name string.
A name string of arbitrary length has already been allocated.
The pointer member is guaranteed to be `NULL`.
questions.answer: The pointer member exists, but it does not automatically point to a separately allocated name string.
questions.explanation: Allocating the structure allocates storage for the pointer member itself, not for the object it might later designate. The program must initialize and allocate the pointed-to resource separately.

questions.prompt: Why initialize nested pointer members to `NULL` immediately after allocating a structure?
options: So cleanup can safely release resources that were acquired before a later failure.
So every pointer automatically receives allocated storage.
So `free` will recursively release all members.
questions.answer: So cleanup can safely release resources that were acquired before a later failure.
questions.explanation: A partially constructed structure may have some members allocated and others not. Initializing pointers to `NULL` lets a cleanup helper call `free` on each member safely.

questions.prompt: What is the correct cleanup order for an owning structure with separately allocated members?
options: Release owned nested allocations, then release the outer structure.
Release the outer structure first and then access its pointer members.
Free only the outer structure; C recursively frees its members.
questions.answer: Release owned nested allocations, then release the outer structure.
questions.explanation: The outer structure contains the pointers needed to reach the nested resources. Release those owned resources before freeing the structure itself.

questions.prompt: A program allocates an array of five structures. What does one successful `free(array)` release?
options: The array allocation itself, but not separate allocations referenced by pointer members.
The array and every allocation referenced by all pointer members.
questions.answer: The array allocation itself, but not separate allocations referenced by pointer members.
questions.explanation: C does not recursively free pointer members. Every separately allocated resource needs its own ownership and cleanup step.

questions.prompt: Which design helps prevent leaks when the second nested allocation fails?
options: Initialize owned pointers to `NULL` and call a cleanup helper that releases every resource already acquired.
Return immediately without freeing the first successful allocation.
Overwrite all pointer members with arbitrary non-null values.
questions.answer: Initialize owned pointers to `NULL` and call a cleanup helper that releases every resource already acquired.
questions.explanation: A cleanup helper can safely free `NULL` members and release earlier successful allocations. This makes partial-construction failure paths manageable.
